content: Noise, in its general usage, refers to any unwanted sound or sound pollution. In the context of electronics, noise can describe the electronic signal that corresponds to acoustic noise, such as in an audio system, or the electronic signal that corresponds to visual noise, often seen as snow on a degraded television or video image. In signal processing or computing, noise is considered data without meaning—data that does not transmit a signal but is instead an unwanted by-product of other activities. However, in Information Theory, noise is still regarded as a form of information. In a broader sense, noise can encompass phenomena such as film grain or even advertisements on web pages. Noise has the potential to block, distort, or alter the meaning of a message in both human and electronic communication. A specific type of noise, known as thermal noise, arises in many of these contexts. Thermal noise sets a fundamental lower limit on what can be measured or signaled and is related to basic physical processes at the molecular level, as described by well-established thermodynamic principles. Some of these principles can be expressed through relatively simple and well-known formulas. Acoustic Noise When discussing noise in relation to sound, it typically refers to meaningless sounds of greater-than-usual volume. For example, loud activities may be described as noisy. Conversations among other people may be perceived as noise by those not involved, and noise can include any unwanted sound, such as barking dogs, neighbors playing loud music, road traffic, chainsaws, or aircraft, which disrupt the tranquility of the countryside. Historically, in 1928/1929, noise was defined as non-speech or natural sound, and in some cases, noise (especially asynchronous use with images) was preferred over synchronized dialogue in moving images. This perspective suggested that noise might have a more significant role in the future. For instance, sound cartoons using real noises were seen as pointing to intriguing possibilities. Alberto Cavalcanti referred to noise as a synonym for natural sound in 1939, and as late as 1960, Siegfried Kracauer described noise as non-speech sound. Audio Noise In audio systems, recording, and broadcasting, audio noise refers to the residual low-level sound, such as hiss and hum, that is audible during quiet periods of a program. In audio engineering, it also refers to unwanted residual electronic noise signals that produce acoustic noise, often heard as hiss. This signal noise is commonly measured using A-weighting or ITU-R 468 weighting. Electronic Noise Electronic noise is present in all circuits and devices due to thermal noise, also known as Johnson Noise. Semiconductor devices can also contribute flicker noise and generation-recombination noise. In any electronic circuit, random variations in current or voltage occur due to the random movement of electrons carrying the current, as they are agitated by thermal energy. Lower temperatures result in reduced thermal noise. This phenomenon limits the minimum signal level that any radio receiver can effectively respond to, as there will always be a small but significant amount of thermal noise in its input circuits. This is why radio telescopes, which search for extremely low-level signals from stars, use front-end low-noise amplifier circuits, typically mounted on the antenna dish and cooled with liquid nitrogen. Uses of Noise Loud noise can be used as a deterrent to ward off unwanted animals or humans. For example, in 1998, actress Barbara Streisand and actor James Brolin used large external speakers outside the tent where they were married to blast very loud heavy metal music outward. This was done to deter journalists and paparazzi from approaching their location.
